findings.where: The full-bleed house-blue band straight after the first screen ('Get Mark's briefings on PPP reform' with a white Subscribe button), desktop and phone
findings.fault: The page's biggest, most saturated surface is given to a secondary action. The palette gives blue one job, 'the action on the first screen', and that action is a small blue box. A whole blue field then comes straight after the slate hero, so the strongest colour on the page points at Subscribe, not at writing to Mark. The slate meets a full field of pure blue with nothing between them, which also turns a quiet slate-and-paper page into a two-field page. That is v5's lever (one blue field), not v7's 'one quiet contact'.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for one action and a single accent. A development-bank visitor who scrolls once also objects: the loudest colour now says 'subscribe', and the quiet personal address Mark wants used reads as the lesser option.

findings.where: The PDF card in the article specimen ('Streamlining the PPP Process… PDF'), desktop and phone
findings.fault: This one resting card stacks every surface signal at once. It has a pale blue fill that is in no palette swatch, a saturated blue 1 px border, a wide soft drop shadow and rounded corners. Every other surface on the page has square corners, no shadow and either grey hairlines or no edge (the swatches, the action box, the Subscribe button, the photos, the motion frame). The house rule bans a hairline border with a wide soft shadow on one resting element, and bans a strong border on top of a fill. The tint is also an untokened colour. The card reads as a web-app widget dropped into a legal journal.
findings.who_objects: Angélique, who will add one of these for every PDF and has no token for the tint. The founder too: the brief asks for the PDF list to read as the product, set as seriously as the article. This card reads slick, which the research names as a failure.

findings.where: The logo lockup in the hero nav (arches and 'MMM INFRA' in warm white on slate), desktop and phone
findings.fault: The client's logo is recoloured. The grey arches and the blue wordmark are both turned warm white, and Mark holds no reversed version. The house rule says a version the client does not hold is made only with his yes. Where the logo fails on a ground, the version or the ground changes, never the logo's colours. Unlike v4, the brief gives v7 no reversed mark, and the palette note states the reversal as settled.
findings.who_objects: Mark, whose logo it is. A lockup he has never approved sits in the first thing he sees, and the founder would be showing him a reversal the house had no licence to make.

findings.where: The 'PALETTE' section label (blue, tracked capitals) and the blue list numbers in the article specimen
findings.fault: Blue is used on text that cannot be clicked. The page's own note says 'Grey for reading, blue only where something can be clicked', and the parts map shows the PALETTE label is static. Every other section label (Type pair, Texture, An article page, Motion sketch) is grey, so this one label is treated unlike its peers. The blue list numerals also give link colour to plain text.
findings.who_objects: A reader who has learned on this page that blue means a link, and finds a blue label and blue numbers that do nothing. Also the founder, who will see the tile break the colour rule it states.
